common_name: Waterleaf (Gbure, West African Talinum Leaf Vegetable)

planting.note: Direct sow or set out rooted cuttings once soil is warm and all frost danger has passed; waterleaf thrives in hot, humid conditions and grows fastest during the peak of Gulf Coast summer.

directions: Sow seed shallowly or root stem cuttings directly in fertile, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to light shade, keeping the bed consistently damp since this succulent-leaved green wilts quickly in dry conditions. Waterleaf, known as gbure in Yoruba and grown widely across West Africa, is a fast-growing, heat-loving leafy green with thick, glossy, mildly mucilaginous leaves used much like spinach in soups and stews, most famously in Nigerian edikang ikong soup. The plant grows as a spreading, succulent-stemmed perennial in frost-free climates but is easily grown as a warm-season annual elsewhere, tolerating both the intense heat and humidity of a Gulf Coast summer that stresses many temperate greens. Harvest by pinching young stem tips and leaves regularly, which encourages new branching and keeps a steady supply of tender growth; plants regrow quickly after cutting.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8–10 weeks before the last frost, since Capsicum chinense types are slow to germinate and mature; transplant into warm, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay above 60°F.

directions: Start seed indoors well ahead of the season, since Capsicum chinense types germinate slowly and need a long, hot growing season to fully ripen; transplant into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun once the weather is reliably warm. Congo Pepper is a traditional Trinidad and Tobago chile closely related to the island's famous Trinidad Scorpion and Moruga Scorpion lines, producing wrinkled, lantern-shaped pods that ripen from green through yellow, orange, and finally deep red, carrying extreme superhot heat well beyond a habanero. Beneath the heat is a distinctly fruity, almost tropical flavor that makes it prized in Trinidadian pepper sauces and hot sauce blends despite its intensity. Handle ripe fruit with gloves, since the capsaicin level is high enough to cause skin irritation, and harvest as pods fully color for the best flavor and heat development.

common_name: Hungarian Black Pepper (Cold-Hardy Purple-Black Ornamental Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Hungarian Black tolerates cooler temperatures than most peppers and can be set out slightly earlier than tender tropical types.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun, well-drained soil after the coldest weather has passed. Hungarian Black is a dual-purpose ornamental and culinary pepper with striking deep purple flowers and foliage that darkens to near-black, setting slender purple-black fruit that ripens through purple to bright red, giving the plant multicolor visual interest across a single growing season. Fruit carries mild to medium heat, roughly comparable to a jalapeño, and is entirely usable in the kitchen even though the plant is most often grown for its dramatic dark coloring in ornamental beds and containers. Among peppers it is notably more tolerant of cool temperatures than typical tropical types, allowing a slightly earlier transplant date and better performance into cool fall weather. Harvest at any color stage; purple fruit is milder and firmer, while fully red fruit is sweeter and slightly hotter.
sources: Cornell University Vegetable Varieties for Gardeners

common_name: Chinese Five-Color Pepper (Multicolor Ornamental Hot Pepper)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6–8 weeks before the last frost and transplant into well-drained, fertile soil in full sun once nights stay above 55°F.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into full sun, well-drained soil after frost danger passes. Chinese Five-Color is a compact ornamental hot pepper prized for producing small, upward-facing fruit in purple, cream, yellow, orange, and red all at once on the same plant, since individual peppers ripen through this color sequence at slightly different rates, creating a constantly shifting, jewel-like display against the plant's purple-tinged green foliage and purple flowers. The small, tapered fruit carries real heat in the cayenne range and is fully edible, useful in hot sauces or pickling, though most growers treat the plant primarily as a container or bedding ornamental. The compact, well-branched habit needs no staking and performs equally well in the ground or in a decorative pot on a sunny patio; harvest fruit at any color stage once past the initial pale coloring.
